new_statements.quote: De medeklinkers die in de beide talen voorkomen zijn b, mb, d, nd, g, j, k, l, m, n, n̯, p, t en w; in M. vinden we bovendien nog f, h, ng, en s; bij de groepen Nggarum en Jabége treedt r op i. p. v. l. De betoning van de syllaben is niet sterk (ongeveer als in het Maleis); wanneer we het nuttig oordelen ze aan te geven, doen we dat met een accent grave.
new_statements.translation: The consonants that occur in both languages are b, mb, d, nd, g, j, k, l, m, n, n̯, p, t and w; in M[aklew] we additionally find f, h, ng, and s; in the Nggarum and Jabége groups r appears instead of l. The stressing of the syllables is not strong (roughly as in Malay); when we judge it useful to indicate it, we do so with a grave accent.
new_statements.citation: Drabbe, Peter. 1950. Talen en Dialecten van Zuid-West Nieuw-Guinea. Anthropos 45(4-6): 545-574.

De beton…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Drabbe states only that syllable stress in Maklew (and Yelmek) is weak, comparable to Malay, and gives no rule for its position; he marks stress ad hoc with a grave accent on individual forms. In his Maklew wordlist (pp. 566-574) the graves fall on varying syllables — often the first syllable of disyllables (òpo 'eye', ùho 'mouth', mìda 'chin', bìla 'throat', mòmo 'breast', mbàku 'nape', hìmo 'buttocks') but also medial (pndàpna 'side', ongokòwo 'gall') and final (Mawèk, the Maklew name of the Bulaka river) — so no fixed position can be read off the source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Maklew (a 'bijtoon' on the final syllable is mentioned only for Mombum, p. 561-562, a different language).
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress marking is explicitly selective ('when we judge it useful').
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic remark on word/citation forms elicited from young Maklew speakers at the Merauke mission boarding school (1946-47); Drabbe never visited Welbuti. For the sister language Yelmek, the modern instrumental description (Gregor 2021: 62-64) finds no conclusive evidence of word-level stress, with prominence drifting toward the end of the word/phrase — consistent with Drabbe's 'weak stress' remark but not a statement about Maklew.
new_statements.identity_note: Drabbe's §2 statement is made jointly for 'Jélmèk' (Yelmek, Ilwayab/Jélwajab variety; yelm1242) and 'Maklew' (Welbuti; makl1246); his Maklew data came from Welbuti-born boarding-school pupils in Merauke. Gregor 2021's 'no word-level stress' finding is for Wanam Yelmek (yelm1242), not Maklew, and is cited here only as sister-language context.

sources.note: p. 549 §2 'Klinkers en Medeklinkers' (joint for Jélmèk and Maklew): syllable stress is not strong (roughly as in Malay); marked with a grave accent only where deemed useful. No location rule. Graves on Maklew items in the wordlist (pp. 566-574) sit on varying syllables (òpo, ùho, mìda, bìla, mòmo, mbàku, hìmo, pndàpna, ongokòwo, Mawèk). (Contrast: for Mombum, p. 561-562, Drabbe does give a rule — mostly final, trisyllables initial — but that is a different language.)

sources.citation: Gregor, Tina. 2021. A documentation and description of Yelmek. PhD thesis, Australian National University (hdl:1885/220032), xx+457 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Describes Wanam Yelmek only (sister language): §3.6/3.6.1 pp. 62-64 'no evidence for lexical tone or contrastive stress.. no conclusive evidence for word-level stress in Yelmek and I thus assume there is none'; prominence tends to rise toward the end of the word/phrase. Maklew appears only in lexical/historical comparison (ch. 2) and a recorded wordlist (PARADISEC TG2); no Maklew prosody statement. Confirms (p. 12) that Drabbe 1950 and Boelaars 1950 are the only grammatical accounts of Maklew.
